Corinth. Perched on the isthmus connecting mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, it was a wealthy maritime and commercial hub that rivaled Athens and Sparta in influence and prosperity. Its position made it an invaluable gateway for trade and military movement, and its cultural achievements shaped early Greek art.

Corinth was located on the isthmus between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese, controlling the only land passage between them and commanding two harbors—Lechaeum and Cenchreae. This position meant the city dominated trade routes and became the wealthiest city-state of its time. It established colonies across the Mediterranean in Sicily, the Adriatic, and Egypt.

The city hosted the Isthmian Games, one of the four great Greek athletic festivals, held every two years in honor of Poseidon. Corinth pioneered Corinthian pottery, distinguished by its elaborate black-figure decoration, and exported ceramics across the known world. The city developed the Corinthian Order of columns, noted for its elaborate capitals decorated with acanthus leaves—the most ornate of the three classical orders. Corinthian architecture became synonymous with sophistication and luxury.

Atop the acropolis stood a sanctuary of Aphrodite that was famed for its courtesans. The city was destroyed by Rome in 146 BCE as punishment for resisting Roman dominance, but was refounded a century later as a Roman colony. Athens and Sparta were rival city-states, occasional allies to Corinth. According to some accounts, Perseus, after slaying Medusa, came to rule Corinth. Jason, the leader of the Argonauts, was sometimes said to have ruled Corinth as well. Poseidon, honored at the Isthmian Games, held a special place in the city's religious life.
